Note to self: difference between DPO and Reinforce

The loss function in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is given by \[ \mathcal L_{DPO} = -E_{(c, y^+, y^-)\sim D^{\text{train}}} [\sigma(\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y^+ | c)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^+ | c)}) - \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y^- | c)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^- | c)})]. \] The weight updates leaves the distribution \(D^{train}\) untouched.

At other times, we may be interested in optimizing \[ J(\theta) = E_{y\sim\pi_{\theta (\cdot \mid c)}}[R(c,y)]. \] The immediate obstacle is that sampling distribution now depends on \(\theta\). To address this, note that \[ \nabla J(\theta) = \sum_{y}R(c,y)\nabla_\theta \pi_{\theta}(y \mid c) = E_{y\sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid c)}[R(c,y)\nabla_\theta\log(\pi_\theta (y \mid c))], \] where the last equality follows from the trick that \(\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta}f_\theta(x) = f_\theta(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \log(f_\theta(x))\), under suitable regularity conditions. The good news is that we now can estimate \(\nabla J(\theta)\) by sampling over \(y\sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid c)\), rather than emumerating over the potentially monstrous \(y\).

Knowing the “log-trick” is not strictly necccesary for discovering this useful computation trick. Once we turn to the sampling strategy for estimating \(\sum_{y}R(c,y)\nabla_\theta \pi_{\theta}(y \mid c)\), the following inverse propensity weighting estimator is almost second nature: \[ E_{y\sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid c)}[R(c,y) \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta (y\mid c)}{\pi_\theta(y\mid c)}]. \] Since \(\frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta (y\mid c)}{\pi_\theta(y\mid c)} =\nabla_\theta\log(\pi_\theta (y \mid c))\), our expression and that appeared in REINFORCE are mathematically equivalent. However, the inverse propensity weighting apporach can be numerically unstable, for reasons that goes beyond this post.

While here we presented a fixed context/prompt \(c\), in general we assume the context distribution of \(c\) to be fixed, and extension to such case is straightfoward.
